title: Chapter XII

teacherSummary.text: Hidden, the creature observes the De Lacey family: the blind old father, Felix and Agatha. Seeing their poverty, he stops stealing their food and secretly gathers firewood for them. He begins to understand speech. Catching sight of his reflection in a pool, he is horrified at his own appearance.

vocabulary.context: “These thoughts exhilarated me, and led me to apply with fresh ardour to the acquiring the art of language.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “exhilarate”: ex- (Latin ex, "out of") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: A person appointed, or chosen, by parties to determine a controversy between them
vocabulary.context: I looked upon them as superior beings, who would be the arbiters of my future destiny.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “arbiter”: -er (Old English -ere, "one who"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: It was as the ass and the lapdog; yet surely the gentle ass whose intentions were affectionate, although his manners were rude, deserved better treatment than blows and execration.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “execration”: ex- (Latin ex, "out of") + -ation (Latin -atio, "the act or result of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: The gentle manners and beauty of the cottagers greatly endeared them to me: when they were unhappy, I felt depressed; when they rejoiced, I sympathised in their joys.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “endear”: en- (French en-/Latin in-, "into"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: I saw few human beings beside them; and if any other happened to enter the cottage, their harsh manners and rude gait only enhanced to me the superior accomplishments of my friends.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “enhance”: en- (French en-/Latin in-, "into"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The act of uttering with articulation
vocabulary.context: Their pronunciation was quick; and the words they uttered, not having any apparent connection with visible objects, I was unable to discover any clue by which I could unravel the mystery of their reference.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “pronunciation”: pro- (Latin pro, "forward, for") + -ation (Latin -atio, "the act or result of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To bestow attention, care, and labor upon, with a view to valuable returns
vocabulary.context: I observed, with pleasure, that he did not go to the forest that day, but spent it in repairing the cottage, and cultivating the garden.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “cultivate”: -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The light given by the stars
vocabulary.context: When they had retired to rest, if there was any moon, or the night was starlight, I went into the woods, and collected my own food and fuel for the cottage.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “starlight”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: An opinion, or judgment, formed on defective or presumptive evidence
vocabulary.context: I conjectured, therefore, that he found on the paper signs for speech which he understood, and I ardently longed to comprehend these also; but how was that possible, when I did not even understand the sounds for which they stood as signs?
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “conjecture”: con- (Latin com-, "with, together") + ject (Latin iacere, "to throw") + -ure (Latin -ura, "act, result"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: I found that these people possessed a method of communicating their experience and feelings to one another by articulate sounds.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “communicate”: com- (Latin com-, "with, together") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: The cottage represents the domestic ideal praised in the Preface.

significance: The creature's kindness shows his capacity for virtue before rejection hardens him.
discussionQuestions: What does the creature's secret help reveal about his nature?
Where does characterization appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with isolation and the need for companionship?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XII,” how does Shelley show learning compassion by watching? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter XII, how does Shelley develop the idea of learning compassion by watching? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the characterization in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XII develops the idea of learning compassion by watching. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and setting shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter XII (where it begins, turns and ends) and its characterization shape the reader's understanding of learning compassion by watching. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter XII suggests about learning compassion by watching. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's characterization and setting), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary Shelley uses characterization in Chapter XII to complicate the reader's understanding of learning compassion by watching. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XII within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of learning compassion by watching responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter XII alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of learning compassion by watching follows or bends those conventions, using the characterization as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter XII and its treatment of learning compassion by watching. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's characterization and setting, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter XII as evidence for a larger claim about learning compassion by watching in Frankenstein. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XII as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of learning compassion by watching. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Frankenstein.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: What does the creature's secret help reveal about his nature? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are exhilarated, arbiters, execration, endeared, enhanced. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: ““These thoughts exhilarated me, and led me to apply with fresh ardour to the acquiring the art of language.” Webster's says: To make merry or jolly. Now the word history: “exhilarate”: ex- (Latin ex, "out of") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “arbiter”: -er (Old English -ere, "one who"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “execration”: ex- (Latin ex, "out of") + -ation (Latin -atio, "the act or result of"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Frankenstein would have known. The cottage represents the domestic ideal praised in the Preface. Why does this chapter matter? The creature's kindness shows his capacity for virtue before rejection hardens him. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see characterization, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to learning compassion by watching.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Setting, Theme.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: “I remember, the first time that I did this, the young woman, when she opened the door in the morning, appeared greatly astonished on seeing a great pile of wood on the outside. She uttered some words in a loud voice, and the youth joined her, who also expressed surprise. I observed, with pleasure, that he did not go to the forest that day, but spent it in repairing the cottage, and cultivating the garden.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Characterization, Setting, Theme: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter XII,” how does Shelley show learning compassion by watching? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to the costs of unchecked ambition? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about learning compassion by watching, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how characterization shapes learning compassion by watching. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
